text: Prior work bearing on these hypotheses is thin and mostly general. Reviews of misinformation describe its spread and influence as a feature of the post-truth information environment (Lewandowsky et al., 2017). Reviews of conspiracy theories ask which factors are associated with conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019), which is relevant to the hypotheses about sharers who believe disputed claims. A cross-national study of COVID-19 misinformation examines predictors of belief in common false statements and links such belief to health behaviours (Roozenbeek et al., 2020). None of these works estimates how sharer attributes such as tie strength, trust, ideology, origin or knowledge affect willingness to share or the perceived plausibility of a post. The retrieved works do not directly disagree with one another or with the study's expectations, because none tests the same source-attribute effects. The nearest tension lies between accounts in which belief in misinformation drives behaviour (Roozenbeek et al., 2020) and the study's interest in sharing without believing (X4), in which sharing and plausibility judgments may come apart. The study's design, with randomized profile features and separate sharing and plausibility outcomes, can speak to that question. It cannot adjudicate the broader accounts of why people hold conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019).
